controls.label: Color + brightness
controls.qualification: The star's color, darker where TESS saw it dimmer (contrast drawn stronger) · March and April 2026, mapped in this project
controls.notes: PDS 70 in its own color, darker where its light in TESS's images of March and April 2026 says it was darker. As the star turned once in 3.06 days its light rose and fell by 14%. The contrast is drawn far stronger than it is, so the eye can see it: the darkest part gives 60.4% less light than the brightest, and is drawn as a much darker tone of the star's own hue; the Brightness map's scale has the measured values. The longitudes of the darker and brighter parts are measured. Their latitudes and shapes are not: they are the smoothest that reproduce the light. No change of color is drawn, because none is measured. Spots come and go within weeks or months: this is the star then. The darkening toward the edge is the Color dataset's limb law, drawn 1.5 times as strong.

controls.label: Brightness map
controls.qualification: Mapped in this project · TESS mission light curve, sector 11
controls.notes: Where the star's surface was darker and brighter in TESS sector 11, worked out in this project from how its light rose and fell by 14% as it turned once in 3.06 days. The light curve is the mission's own; the criteria of Holcomb et al. (2022, ApJ 936, 138) decide that it shows the star turning, and starry finds the map that reproduces it. The longitudes of the dark and bright regions are fixed by the data; their latitudes are not. The map is made at a tilt of 55°, worked out from the star's rotation speed, period and radius. Step through the 2 maps to see the spots change.
controls.legendNote: Darker: dimmer than the star's mean surface; white: brighter.

controls.label: Color
controls.qualification: Color from the star's X-shooter spectrum; darkening toward the edge from a model atmosphere. The disc itself is unresolved.
controls.notes: The color of the star's spectrum measured with ESO's X-shooter on 26 December 2020, through a slit wide enough to keep all its light: an orange K7 star. It is still accreting gas from its disc, and that light is part of its color. The darkening toward the edge is the quadratic law Claret and Bloemen (2011) compute from ATLAS model atmospheres for a star of 3,972 K and log g 4.22: a model, because no image measures this star's limb. No spin axis is measured on the sky, so the display axis is celestial north.

controls.label: Dust ring · ALMA 0.87 mm
controls.notes: The star in the color of its spectrum, with the ring of dust around it in its own glow at 0.87 millimetres, as ALMA imaged it on 27 July 2019 (project 2018.A.00030.S). It is the ALMA pipeline's image from the public archive, shown in the color map and scale Benisty et al. (2021) use in their Figure 1. The ring lies 50 to 100 au from the star, outside the orbits of planets b (21 au) and c (34 au), which have cleared the gap inside it; it is brighter on its north-west side. Measured on this image it is 73.5 au in radius and tilted 50°, against 74 au and 51.7° in Keppler et al. (2019). The image has no third axis, so the depth is inferred: a tilted ring of that geometry projects to it better than a spherical shell or a constant depth, and each line of sight is placed on it. Its west side is drawn nearer, the side Keppler et al. (2018) find nearer in scattered light; its thickness is a stated convention. The faint dust around planet c that Benisty et al. found is at the edge of this image's noise and is not claimed.
